subtopic: Drawn into a high-control group or online extremism
passage:
Jamal's first month at university in Manchester was the loneliest of his life. Rain, a single room, a kettle, and a flatmate he'd seen twice.
So when a friendly group at the student fair invited him to their Thursday dinners, he almost said yes on the spot. Free food, warm people, someone asking his name twice so they'd remember it.
Instead he went once, and on the second visit he asked the organiser, Hannah, some questions. 'Who pays for the dinners? Who runs it? What happens if someone stops coming?'
Hannah didn't blink. 'The student union gives us a small grant, it's on the website. A committee of five, elected each year. And people drop in and out all the time. No hard feelings.'
That evening he told Bilal on their weekly video call back home in Leeds. 'They answered everything,' he said. 'I'll keep going. But you're still my Sunday call, yeah?'

qa.q: Who did Jamal call every week?
qa.a: Jamal called Bilal on their weekly video call.

qa.q: Why did Jamal almost say yes on the spot?
qa.a: He felt very lonely in his first month, so warm people and free food were hard to resist.

qa.q: Which of Jamal's choices were wise, and why?
qa.a: He asked who pays, who runs it and what happens if you leave, and kept his weekly call with Bilal; open answers and outside friends protect against being drawn into an unhealthy group.

qa.q: How might Hannah see Jamal's questions?
qa.a: Hannah treats them as normal and reasonable, which is itself a good sign about the group.

grounding: It shows a lonely young man asking about a group's money, leadership and leaving, finding open answers, and keeping in touch with an outside friend.

The orientation hall of the engineering college still had banners from the freshers' welcome. Madhav, nineteen and far from home for the first time, had spent most evenings alone in his hostel room.
So when Shankar, a final-year student, invited him to a 'leadership fellowship', he went. The seniors were warm. They remembered his hometown. They offered to help with assignments.
At the second meeting, Madhav asked, 'Who funds this? Who's the head? And if I leave after a month, is that okay?'
The room went quiet. Shankar smiled, but his voice cooled. 'Those questions show a lack of trust, Madhav. The fellowship is for people who are all in.'
Madhav felt his face heat up. He said he'd think about it.
That night he knocked on the door of Vikas, his old school friend two floors down, and they walked to the canteen for chai. He didn't go to the third meeting.

qa.q: Who invited Madhav to the leadership fellowship?
qa.a: Shankar, a final-year student, invited him.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when Shankar called his questions a lack of trust?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and uneasy, his face heating up, and sensed something was wrong.

qa.q: What did Madhav do well in dealing with the fellowship?
qa.a: He asked about money, leaders and leaving, read the cold reaction as a warning sign, and reconnected with an old friend instead of going back.

qa.q: How might Vikas see Madhav's late-night knock?
qa.a: Vikas may simply be glad to see an old friend, and that company gives Madhav a safe, ordinary place to belong.

grounding: It shows a lonely student asking about a group's funding, leaders and rules on leaving, and stepping back when questions are treated as disloyalty.
